paras: The lynching of Julian Medon was the hanging of a young Mexican man whose body was found on a tree at Moore's Hill, eleven miles south of Mariposa, California, in late January 1888. The case drew renewed notice in July 1888, when three men were jailed as suspects in what a press dispatch called "plainly a case of lynching."

On a Tuesday morning in late January 1888, about January 24, the body of a Mexican was found hanging to a tree at Moore Hill in southern Mariposa County. The first brief gave his name as "Julian Leden" and added, without naming a source, that he "had been engaged in stealing cattle." A later Mariposa dispatch gave the name as Julian Medon. No report of an inquest appears in the coverage.

According to the July dispatch, suspicion had fallen on several cattlemen, and county officers were censured for their lack of activity. They were said to have quietly traced suspects through detectives, though what evidence they held was not disclosed. Jim Westfall and Jack McGuire were arrested in the week before July 19, and a third man, named Smithers, was arrested on July 19; all three were held in jail.
The dispatch reported rumors of further arrests and concluded that some of "the gang" had informed. No report of an examination, indictment or trial of the three men was found.

Both reports of the case ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. In January the paper carried the death as one sentence among its "Telegraphic Brevities" and passed on the cattle-stealing claim as fact without calling the killing a lynching. Six months later a California Associated Press dispatch ran on the front page under the headline "Somebody 'Squealed,'" calling the case a lynching "in a Fair Way of Being Exposed."

That dispatch called the suspects "the guilty parties" but took a light tone, saying Smithers was "bagged" and that rumors pointed to "more recruits for the same institution." Neither report said more about the victim than that he was a Mexican, and the July dispatch did not repeat the earlier cattle-theft remark.

reader.title: Lynching of Julian Medon
bases: A man was found hanging from a tree (A1, A2), and the July dispatch called it 'plainly a case of lynching' and reported the arrest of three suspects (A2).

Medon was found hanged and the July dispatch called the killing a lynching (A1, A2), and the January brief tied him to cattle stealing (A1), which suggests a pretext of punishment; the group size rests only on the arrest of three men and a reference to 'the gang', not on any finding about who hanged him (A2).

Two separate reports six months apart, a January telegraphic brief (A1) and a July California Associated Press dispatch (A2), agree that a young Mexican was found hanging from a tree at Moore('s) Hill in southern Mariposa County, though both ran in the same Sacramento paper.

accounts.gist: The hanging of Julian Medon was plainly a lynching; officers, censured for inaction, had traced suspects through detectives and arrested three men, and some of 'the gang' had evidently informed.

framing.detail: A one-sentence item among 'Telegraphic Brevities' that passed on, as fact, that the dead man had been stealing cattle, without calling the killing a lynching.

Headlined 'Somebody "Squealed"' and 'A Mariposa Lynching Case in a Fair Way of Being Exposed', it called the hanging plainly a lynching and the suspects 'the guilty parties', in a light tone ('bagged', 'more recruits for the same institution').
